<reason>Both sides were sharp and disciplined, but PRO (B) made the debate easier to decide. CON's entire case rested on the claim that "no punitive surcharge for declining" makes telematics unfundable and thus "quietly abolishes" it. PRO neutralized this in two steps: first the dilemma in B2.1–2.2 (if monitoring cuts crashes, the discount funds itself; if it doesn't, the refuser surcharge isn't risk-based), then the direct A1 answer in B4.1 conceding that the unmonitored pool's rate may rise on actual claims experience. That concession shrank the live dispute to a single clause—whether insurers may charge up front, presumptively, for the bare act of declining—and PRO's closing convincingly showed CON had adopted nearly every other "fair term" (resale ban, secondary-use ban, location-scoring bar, behaviour-only factors, rate review). CON landed its best blow late (A4.4–4.5: PRO's end state prices the refuser on group averages, "the costume without the behaviour"), and PRO never squarely answered it, but it isn't fatal because PRO always defended ordinary pooled pricing for the unwatched. CON's closing also skipped PRO's pre-emptive distinction (B5.5) between withholding a claims history and withholding a record of your life, leaving "all underwriting is coercion" as a slightly strawmanned reductio. PRO's broken [C1.x] reference is a minor cost; both sides had equal clipping. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–2.2 plus B4.1: PRO turned CON's own safety claim into a dilemma about how the discount is funded, then answered CON's Q1 with the honest concession that experience-based repricing is allowed, collapsing CON's "abolition" thesis to a dispute over up-front presumptive surcharges—the ground on which PRO's "fine for opting out" framing is strongest.</best_rebuttal>
